hypotheses.title: Requirement-Checklist Extraction Instruction Raises Held-Out Pass Rate
hypotheses.claim: Appending the instruction 'Before writing any code, extract every requirement stated in the task and docstrings into a numbered checklist. Before finishing, verify your implementation against each numbered item and fix any item that fails.' raises a small coding agent's held-out-test pass rate versus a no-instruction baseline on spec-dense tasks.
hypotheses.rationale: Calibration probes show the small model already self-tests what it remembers, so residual failures come from requirements it never extracted from the spec. A forced enumeration step converts implicit spec coverage into an explicit artifact the agent can check against, targeting requirement omission rather than duplicating default self-testing. Checklist-style decomposition is a known scaffold for long-instruction compliance, but its effect on held-out grading of spec-dense coding tasks by small agent models is unmeasured here. Proximity synthesis from hyp-6744be5c7092: Appending the instruction 'Before declaring the task done, re-read the complete task description and every docstring one final time, and for each stated behavior confirm your implementation handles it; fix anything that does not.' raises held-out pass rate versus a no-instruction baseline. (similarity 0.978; method embedding_proximity).
assumptions: Held-out grader tests map one-to-one onto requirements stated in the task prompt and docstrings
The agent complies with the appended instruction and actually writes the checklist
Baseline failures are dominated by omitted requirements rather than algorithmic inability
The extra enumeration step fits within the trial turn and time limits

hypotheses.title: Adversarial Edge-Case Enumeration Instruction Raises Held-Out Pass Rate
hypotheses.claim: Appending the instruction 'After implementing, act as an adversarial tester of your own code: enumerate the boundary and degenerate inputs the specification implies (empty inputs, single elements, ties, exact boundaries, invalid values, duplicates) and execute a check for each before finishing.' raises held-out pass rate versus a no-instruction baseline.
hypotheses.rationale: Held-out graders concentrate their discriminating power in edge cases, while the agent's default ad-hoc tests concentrate on the happy path it just implemented. An explicit adversarial-role instruction with a concrete category list redirects the agent's existing self-testing habit toward the input classes where graders actually differ, rather than adding a new artifact type. Mechanism: reweighting existing verification effort, distinct from checklist (extraction) and test-first (coverage-before-code).
assumptions: Grader failures on baseline arms are concentrated in boundary and degenerate inputs
The category list generalizes across task domains in the suite
Executing per-category checks fits within trial limits

hypotheses.title: Pre-Completion Spec Re-Read Instruction Raises Held-Out Pass Rate
hypotheses.claim: Appending the instruction 'Before declaring the task done, re-read the complete task description and every docstring one final time, and for each stated behavior confirm your implementation handles it; fix anything that does not.' raises held-out pass rate versus a no-instruction baseline.
hypotheses.rationale: Requirement omission is hypothesized to happen at read time: details absorbed early decay from working context by the time the agent finishes. A mandatory final re-read re-surfaces forgotten clauses exactly when the implementation exists to be checked against them, at much lower overhead than test-first or checklist scaffolds. It is the minimal intervention targeting the same failure mode, so it also serves as a dose-response comparison point for heavier scaffolds. hypotheses.title: Spec-Derived Test-First Instruction Raises Held-Out Pass Rate
hypotheses.claim: Appending the instruction 'Before implementing, write executable tests that cover every behavior stated in the task and docstrings, including boundary and error cases. Implement until all of your tests pass, then re-check each stated behavior once more.' raises held-out pass rate versus a no-instruction baseline.
hypotheses.rationale: The agent's default behavior is to test ad hoc after implementing, which samples only the behaviors it happened to encode. Writing tests from the specification before implementation forces spec coverage at the moment attention on the spec is highest, and gives the agent a persistent executable artifact whose failures direct fixes. This differs mechanistically from checklist extraction: coverage is enforced by executable checks rather than prose review.
assumptions: The agent can translate stated behaviors into correct executable tests within trial limits
Self-written tests are faithful to the spec rather than to the agent's own misreading
Time spent writing tests does not push trials past turn or timeout limits

matches.rationale: Under the registered protocol's constraints — all-pass per-trial grading and a hard turn cap — the re-read arm's losses are structurally bounded (one turn, no artifact that can be wrong), while test-first's conversion requires near-perfect fidelity across every self-written test on 10-15 clause specs, and its overhead path can flip baseline passes into candidate fails. Test-first retains the higher ceiling on never-encoded omissions, but ceiling only pays if fidelity is high, which is its own uncertain fundamental. Risk-adjusted for this protocol, re-read wins narrowly. This is proxy judgment about experimental promise, not a measured outcome.
matches.judge_trace: multi_round_debate rounds=2; Weighed: failure polarity (re-read bounded at null vs test-first unbounded below) > ceiling advantage (test-first on never-encoded clauses) because all-pass grading multiplies per-test infidelity across dense specs; overhead risk against measured 5-plus-turn headroom is real but secondary; both share the unmeasured omission-dominance premise, so it cancels.; order_swap forward=hyp-6744be5c7092 reverse=hyp-6744be5c7092; position_stable=true; debate_tier=top
debate_transcript: Advocate (re-read): my mechanism costs one turn and cannot lose a trial to overhead; every point of measured delta is attributable to recovered requirements, not survivorship through the turn cap.

Advocate (test-first): a re-read re-runs the same reader over the same text — the failure that caused the omission recurs on the check. Executable tests externalize the spec so the check is not the reader's memory but a program that fails loudly.
Advocate (re-read): your tests are written by the same misreader; a wrong test entrenches the misreading and can actively lower pass rate. My worst case is a null; yours is negative.

Advocate (test-first): asymmetric ceilings, though: when tests are faithful, I catch never-encoded clauses at implementation time — the class your mechanism concedes it cannot recover. Dense-spec tasks are where the experiment discriminates, and there my coverage compounds while your single re-read saturates.

Skeptic: both mechanisms share the unmeasured premise that omissions dominate baseline failures; they differ on overhead (test-first risks the turn cap on dense tasks — measured headroom is five-plus turns, test-writing plausibly consumes most of it) and on failure polarity (re-read cannot go negative, test-first can).

Judge weighing: expected value favors test-first's higher ceiling on the target failure class; risk-adjusted value narrows because its overhead and shared-blindspot paths are real and its losses are unbounded below, while re-read is bounded but likely small. On a turn-capped protocol the bounded-risk arm wins ties; on ceiling potential test-first leads.

Advocate (test-first): round 1 conceded my higher ceiling; the remaining dispute is risk. The turn-cap risk is measurable and bounded in practice — specs in the target suite fit tests in a handful of asserts, not a test framework — while my upside covers the only failure class the objective names that re-read admits it cannot touch.

Advocate (re-read): the protocol's primary metric is all-pass per trial. A single entrenched wrong test on one clause fails the whole trial exactly like an omission; your compounding coverage buys nothing unless test fidelity is near-perfect across 10-15 clauses, and fidelity is your own uncertain fundamental.

Skeptic: quantify the asymmetry — test-first needs roughly all self-tests faithful for a trial to convert (fidelity^n scaling hurts on dense specs); re-read needs one forgotten-but-encoded clause to exist and be recoverable (probability small but positive per trial). Neither dominates a priori; the deciding facts are the baseline failure profile and observed compliance, both of which only the experiment provides.

Judge: preferring the arm whose losses are structurally bounded and whose mechanism is a pure single manipulation, this match goes narrowly to re-read on risk-adjusted grounds for a turn-capped, all-pass protocol; test-first remains the higher-ceiling candidate if fidelity proves high in transcripts.

Judge review of rounds 1-2: ceiling argument conceded to test-first; risk-boundedness argument conceded to re-read; deciding weight assigned to failure polarity under all-pass grading and the turn cap.
Order-swapped replay:

Advocate (test-first): the objective privileges pass-rate gains on spec-dense tasks; executable spec coverage attacks both omission classes (forgotten and never-encoded), and my artifact directs fixes instead of hoping a re-read notices them.

Advocate (re-read): your attack surface is also larger — every self-written test is a place to encode a misreading, and all-pass grading means one bad test can sink a trial your baseline would have passed.
Advocate (test-first): fidelity risk is real but measurable in transcripts; bounded-but-null is not a virtue if the family's purpose is finding an instruction that moves the metric.
Advocate (re-read): the tournament ranks candidates for a small confirmatory experiment; a bounded arm that cannot regress protects the experiment's informativeness at its sample size.

Skeptic: same cruxes as the reversed pairing — fidelity^n scaling on dense specs versus a small-but-positive recovery probability; the baseline failure profile decides, and it is unmeasured until the de-saturated suite runs.
Judge weighing: no new evidence relative to the mirrored match; position order must not change the verdict.
Advocate (test-first): if transcripts later show high test fidelity, my arm dominates; the tournament should not foreclose the higher-ceiling mechanism on unmeasured fear.
Advocate (re-read): and if fidelity is mediocre, your arm actively harms — the tournament ranks for a small all-pass experiment now, where downside protection is worth more than contingent ceiling.
Skeptic: verdict should mirror the reversed match unless either side produced new evidence this round; none was produced.
Judge: applying identical weights as the mirrored pairing — failure polarity under all-pass grading outweighs contingent ceiling at this protocol's sample size.

matches.rationale: The edge-case enumeration arm (second) carries an executed, self-correcting feedback signal precisely on the input classes where the suite's held-out graders discriminate hardest, while the re-read arm offers broad but weak attentional coverage through the same reading modality that produced the baseline failure. Applicability width does not compensate for signal weakness under all-pass grading. Verdict is proxy judgment of experimental promise, not measurement.
matches.judge_trace: multi_round_debate rounds=2; Weighed executed-feedback strength on applicable failure classes against clause-coverage breadth; grader design (per-requirement, boundary-heavy) tips applicability toward edge-enum; both arms cheap, so overhead and turn-cap considerations were non-factors; shared omission-dominance premise cancels.; order_swap forward=hyp-6208299229f5 reverse=hyp-6208299229f5; position_stable=true; debate_tier=top
debate_transcript: Advocate (re-read): I target the named failure mode directly — requirement omission — while you redirect testing effort toward edge classes and are inert whenever the miss is a whole clause, which the harder suite's breadth-first design makes the modal miss.

Advocate (edge-enum): inert on omissions, yes, but potent on the class you cannot fix: implemented-but-mishandled boundaries. Graders in these suites discriminate on boundary semantics; my six-category sweep executes checks there, where your prose re-read produces no execution at all.
Advocate (re-read): execution without coverage of the right clause is motion, not progress; my mechanism at least re-touches every clause once.

Advocate (edge-enum): re-touching with the same reader repeats the same parse; my checks are behavioral — a wrong boundary FAILS in front of the agent, which is qualitatively stronger feedback than re-reading a sentence it already misread.

Skeptic: the two arms bet on different baseline failure profiles — whole-clause omission (favors re-read, weakly) versus boundary mishandling of implemented clauses (favors edge-enum, strongly when true). Both are cheap; neither risks the turn cap. The suite's grader design (per-requirement tests with heavy boundary content) leans toward the edge-enum bet.

Judge weighing: edge-enum's feedback signal is executed and self-correcting where it applies; re-read's is attentional and bounded. Applicability width favors re-read; signal strength favors edge-enum.

Advocate (edge-enum): calibration already showed the agent self-tests what it implements; the marginal value of re-reading is a second pass of the SAME modality that failed. My instruction changes the modality — from reading to executing adversarial inputs — and modality changes are where small models gain most.

Advocate (re-read): your category list is a fixed prior; the harder suite discriminates on stated-but-unusual rules (tie order, negative-zero, escaping) that are not boundary classes at all. My clause-by-clause pass at least touches those.
Advocate (edge-enum): touching is not testing. And my list ends with the spec's own implied classes — invalid values and duplicates cover most stated error rules in the suite.

Skeptic: decision reduces to signal strength versus clause coverage; the grader design (per-requirement tests, boundary-heavy but including rule-specific behaviors) supports edge-enum on roughly half the requirement types and re-read weakly on all. Executed feedback where applicable beats weak feedback everywhere at all-pass grading only if the applicable set is where trials actually fail.

Judge: edge-enum's executed, self-correcting signal on the grader's most discriminating classes outweighs re-read's broad-but-weak attentional touch; verdict to edge-enum, moderate uncertainty pending the measured baseline failure profile.
Judge: modality-change argument (read -> execute) held up across both rounds and aligns with calibration observations of default self-testing behavior; edge-enum takes the match.
Order-swapped replay:

Advocate (edge-enum): mirrored pairing of the previous match; my case stands — executed adversarial checks on the grader's most discriminating classes beat a second pass of the modality that already failed.
Advocate (re-read): and mine — clause-wide coverage touches rule-specific behaviors your category list never reaches.
Skeptic: no new evidence in this ordering; the cruxes (signal strength where applicable vs weak coverage everywhere) are unchanged.
Judge weighing: order-invariance applies; the executed-feedback argument carried the reversed match and nothing here rebuts it.
Advocate (re-read): final attempt — at all-pass grading, one recovered clause flips a trial; breadth across all clause types maximizes the chance that the one recoverable miss is touched.
Advocate (edge-enum): probability mass matters more than support width: the graders concentrate discriminating tests on executable input classes, and executed failures self-correct within the trial.
Skeptic: unchanged cruxes; verdict should mirror the reversed pairing for order-invariance.
Judge: same weights as the mirrored match; executed feedback on discriminating classes prevails.
Judge: mirrored match confirms edge-enum over re-read; no order effect.

sections.abstract: Appending the instruction 'After implementing, act as an adversarial tester of your own code: enumerate the boundary and degenerate inputs the specification implies (empty inputs, single elements, ties, exact boundaries, invalid values, duplicates) and execute a check for each before finishing.' raises held-out pass rate versus a no-instruction baseline.
sections.contribution: Held-out graders concentrate their discriminating power in edge cases, while the agent's default ad-hoc tests concentrate on the happy path it just implemented. An explicit adversarial-role instruction with a concrete category list redirects the agent's existing self-testing habit toward the input classes where graders actually differ, rather than adding a new artifact type. Mechanism: reweighting existing verification effort, distinct from checklist (extraction) and test-first (coverage-before-code).

sections.abstract: Appending the instruction 'Before writing any code, extract every requirement stated in the task and docstrings into a numbered checklist. Before finishing, verify your implementation against each numbered item and fix any item that fails.' raises a small coding agent's held-out-test pass rate versus a no-instruction baseline on spec-dense tasks.
sections.contribution: Calibration probes show the small model already self-tests what it remembers, so residual failures come from requirements it never extracted from the spec. A forced enumeration step converts implicit spec coverage into an explicit artifact the agent can check against, targeting requirement omission rather than duplicating default self-testing. Checklist-style decomposition is a known scaffold for long-instruction compliance, but its effect on held-out grading of spec-dense coding tasks by small agent models is unmeasured here. Proximity synthesis from hyp-6744be5c7092: Appending the instruction 'Before declaring the task done, re-read the complete task description and every docstring one final time, and for each stated behavior confirm your implementation handles it; fix anything that does not.' raises held-out pass rate versus a no-instruction baseline. (similarity 0.978; method embedding_proximity).

An unexplored region worth flagging for evolution: instructions targeting algorithmic self-doubt (e.g. complexity or invariant checks) would cover the failure class this family ignores.

Advocate (re-read): your tests are written by the same misreader; a wrong test entrenches the misreading and can actively lower pass rate. My worst case is a null; yours is negative.
